prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "ADVANCED MICRO DEVICES INC" (ticker AMD). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: AMD fits most Rule Breaker traits: it is a top dog and first mover in chiplet CPUs, a strong No. 2 in AI accelerators, its shares rose about 182% over the past year, Lisa Su is a celebrated leader, and many commentators call the stock overvalued at about 155 times trailing earnings. The weaker trait is a sustainable advantage in AI, where NVIDIA's CUDA ecosystem still dominates.
summaries.buffett: AMD is a capable, well-run business, but it is a fast-changing, capital-light chip designer with a moat that is real but narrower than NVIDIA's or TSMC's, and it lost money as recently as 2016. At roughly 150 times EV/EBIT and a 0.85% free-cash-flow yield the price offers no margin of safety, so it sits outside Buffett's usual circle of competence and price discipline.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire Lisa Su's rational, execution-focused turnaround and the x86 duopoly, but semiconductors are a field he regarded as hard to predict, and AMD must keep out-engineering NVIDIA, Intel and in-house hyperscaler chips. Inverting, the risks are clear (CUDA lock-in, custom ASICs, TSMC dependence) and the price leaves little room for error.
summaries.lynch: AMD is a classic Lynch fast grower with a simple story (taking server share from Intel and selling AI GPUs to OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic), and its PEG of about 0.84 on forward estimates looks acceptable on paper. Against that, it is one of the most heavily covered stocks on Wall Street, insiders are not buying and the share count has grown, so it lacks Lynch's overlooked-bargain qualities.
summaries.fisher: AMD scores well on Fisher's growth points: a long runway in AI and data centers, a management committed to new products (Zen roadmap, MI300 to MI450, Helios racks), R&D that has produced market-leading chips, and strong customer relationships. Gross margin rose to 50% GAAP in 2025, though operating margins are still diluted by Xilinx amortization.
summaries.graham: AMD fails almost every Graham defensive test: it has never paid a regular dividend in modern times, it lost $497M in 2016, and it trades at about 155 times trailing earnings and 14.7 times book. It is a large company with a strong balance sheet, but nothing about the price meets Graham's conservative criteria.
summaries.thiel: AMD is a strong execution story rather than a monopoly: its chiplet and 3D V-Cache technology is excellent but not ten times better than rivals, and in AI it competes head on with NVIDIA. Its timing in the AI buildout, world-class team under Lisa Su and established distribution to every hyperscaler are strong answers to Thiel's questions; its durability and 'secret' are less clear.
summaries.gerstner: AMD is a direct beneficiary of the AI compute build-out Gerstner focuses on, with multi-gigawatt commitments from OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic and a management target of more than 35% revenue growth a year. The question is price: at about 55 times forward earnings the stock already discounts a lot of that growth.
summaries.druckenmiller: AMD has the earnings momentum and catalysts Druckenmiller looks for: trailing-twelve-month net income of $6.43B versus $4.34B in 2025, rising estimates, and the MI450/Helios ramp starting in the second half of 2026, with the stock up about 182% in a year. The risks are crowded positioning, a 2.45 beta, and dependence on continued AI capital spending.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would see a good but not yet great company: gross margin of about 50% (GAAP, 2025) is solid, but return on invested capital is under 10% after the Xilinx acquisition and the business has been cyclical. With a free-cash-flow yield of about 0.85%, it fails his 'don't overpay' test.
summaries.greenblatt: AMD scores poorly on the Magic Formula: return on capital is under 10% and its earnings yield (EBIT over enterprise value) is under 1% at an EV/EBIT of about 150. It would rank near the bottom of a Greenblatt screen today.
summaries.akre: AMD has a strong business with a long reinvestment runway in AI and data centers and a talented, honest manager in Lisa Su, which covers two legs of Akre's stool. The weak leg is the business's return on capital, which is under 10% today, and the share count has grown rather than shrunk.
summaries.pabrai: AMD is the opposite of a Dhandho bet: there is no distress, the outcome is uncertain, and at about 155 times trailing earnings the downside is large if AI growth disappoints. Pabrai's low-risk, high-uncertainty, buy-cheap approach would not apply here.
summaries.wood: AMD is squarely in ARK's AI platform, selling Instinct accelerators and Helios racks into a market AMD sizes at over $1 trillion by 2030, and AI-PC and embedded edge chips extend that. Its products follow falling cost-per-compute curves, though it is a chip supplier rather than a combiner of several innovation platforms.
summaries.ackman: AMD is a dominant x86 duopolist with a strong balance sheet ($13.1B cash vs $3.2B debt in June 2026), but it is cyclical, capital-intensive at its foundry partner and exposed to export controls, and its earnings are less predictable than the simple, free-cash-flow-generative businesses Pershing Square prefers. The valuation also leaves little room for an Ackman-style discount.
summaries.sleep: AMD does pass some benefits of scale to customers through cheaper performance per dollar than Intel, but it is the challenger in AI, not a 'scale economies shared' leader like Costco or Amazon. Its position in 10-20 years depends on out-innovating NVIDIA and custom chips, which makes it less certain than Sleep's favoured compounders.
summaries.valentine: AMD addresses a huge, painful problem (the shortage and cost of compute for AI and cloud) in a market measured in hundreds of billions of dollars, which is the kind of market Valentine prized. As a 57-year-old public company it is far from a start-up, but its AI business has the large-market, technology-driven profile Sequoia looks for.

momentum.evidence: AMD shares rose 181.77% in the 52 weeks to Oct 13, 2026 (close $605.53), versus a 20.42% one-year total return for the SPY S&P 500 ETF.

g4.evidence: CEO Lisa Su (TIME CEO of the Year 2024) leads AMD, and OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic have signed multi-gigawatt Instinct commitments, with OpenAI's deal tied to warrants for up to 160M AMD shares.

g6.evidence: At about 155 times trailing earnings and 24 times sales (StockAnalysis, Oct 13, 2026) the stock is widely described as expensive, especially after its post-OpenAI-deal rally.

simple.evidence: The business model (design chips, have TSMC make them, sell to PC, server and AI customers) is understandable, but judging chip architectures, AI software ecosystems and product cycles is hard for a generalist.

b2.evidence: Revenue grew from $9.76B in 2020 to $34.64B in 2025, but it fell in 2023 and AMD posted a $497M net loss in 2016.

integrity.evidence: Lisa Su sets public long-term targets (more than 35% revenue CAGR) and has largely hit her roadmaps, though heavy stock compensation and acquisition-related share issuance dilute owners.

b6.evidence: Acquisitions such as Xilinx, Pensando, ZT Systems and Silo AI fit AMD's data-center strategy rather than being empire-building, but the Xilinx deal added years of amortization and lifted diluted shares from 1,229M in 2021 to 1,571M in 2022.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital was about 9.8% on a trailing basis (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), held back by the goodwill and intangibles from the all-stock Xilinx acquisition, though AMD carries little debt.

fcf.evidence: In 2025 AMD generated $5,519M of free cash flow against $4,335M of GAAP net income.

b10.evidence: AMD pays no dividend and reinvested its profits, and its market value rose to about $989B by October 2026 from a near-bankrupt company in 2014, far more than the earnings it retained.

safety.evidence: At $605.53 the stock trades at about 155 times trailing EPS of $3.90 and 14.7 times book value, well above any conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: The forward P/E of about 55 is high, but with consensus FY2026 revenue growth of about 47% the forward PEG ratio is about 0.84 (StockAnalysis).

mu5.evidence: The x86 duopoly and $13.1B cash pile limit the risk of failure, but AMD could still lose ground to NVIDIA's CUDA, custom ASICs, Arm CPUs or a TSMC supply disruption in Taiwan.

reinvest.evidence: AMD can pour profits into AI GPUs, rack-scale systems and server CPUs, where management targets data-center revenue growth above 60% a year for 3-5 years.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower with a simple story: taking server CPU share from Intel (about 34.5% unit share in Q2 2026) and selling AI GPUs to OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 155 is far above past growth, but on forward estimates the PEG ratio is about 0.84, below 1.

runway.evidence: AMD sizes the data-center AI accelerator market at over $1 trillion by 2030 and has multi-year deployments with OpenAI (6 GW), Meta (6 GW) and Anthropic (up to 2 GW).

ly7.evidence: Insiders such as Lisa Su sell stock under trading plans rather than buying, and the share count rose about 1.1% over the past year despite $1,316M of buybacks in 2025.

ly8.evidence: AMD is one of the most heavily traded and covered stocks in the market, with dozens of analysts publishing estimates.

fi2.evidence: AMD has released Zen 1 through Zen 5 CPUs on schedule since 2017 and moved from MI300 to MI355X and MI450/Helios racks, while CPU lines mature.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced the chiplet and 3D V-Cache designs behind EPYC's server share gains and the Ryzen X3D gaming CPUs, and chips that power the El Capitan and Frontier supercomputers.

fi4.evidence: AMD has won every major cloud provider for EPYC and signed giant AI deals, but in PCs and gaming GPUs it often has to price below Intel and NVIDIA to win share.

longterm.evidence: Lisa Su committed to the multi-year Zen and chiplet bets from 2014 and invested in AI GPUs for years before the MI300 paid off in 2024.

gr1.evidence: AMD had $34.64B of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $989B in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: AMD reported a GAAP net loss of $497M in 2016, within the last ten years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS went from a loss of $0.60 in 2016 to a profit of $2.65 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: At $605.53 the price is about 155 times trailing EPS of $3.90 and far higher on average earnings of recent years ($1.00 in 2024, $2.65 in 2025).

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 155 times P/B of about 14.7 gives a product above 2,000, far beyond Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: EPYC and Instinct chips are competitive or leading on some benchmarks, but they are not ten times better than Intel Xeon or NVIDIA Blackwell.

timing.evidence: The AI data-center build-out arrived just as AMD's MI300/MI355X GPUs matured, and MI450/Helios racks start shipping in 2H 2026 for OpenAI and Meta.

th3.evidence: AMD started as Intel's second source and rebuilt from about 5.8% server share in 2020 to 34.5% in 2026, but it never held a big share of a small market.

team.evidence: Lisa Su, an MIT PhD who led AMD from 2014, and her team engineered one of the best turnarounds in tech history.

th5.evidence: AMD sells through every major PC maker (Dell, HP, Lenovo), every big cloud provider and Sony and Microsoft consoles, and added rack-scale system capability via ZT Systems.

durable.evidence: The x86 franchise and design know-how should last, but Arm CPUs and custom AI chips from Google, Amazon and Broadcom threaten its markets over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: AMD saw earlier than Intel that chiplets on TSMC's leading nodes would beat monolithic chips, but that insight is now widely copied.

trend.evidence: AMD is the main merchant alternative to NVIDIA for AI accelerators and a leading supplier of server CPUs for cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Trailing-twelve-month net income reached $6.43B by June 2026 versus $4,335M for 2025, and analysts raised price targets in October 2026 (Citi to $800, Mizuho to $705).

dr2.evidence: The MI450/Helios ramp for OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic should lift results through 2027, but consensus already expects FY2027 revenue of about $89B, so much is priced in.

dr4.evidence: Hyperscaler and AI-lab capital spending remains strong, but as a 2.45-beta growth stock AMD is sensitive to interest rates and any tightening in AI funding.

dr6.evidence: First MI450/Helios deliveries in 2H 2026, Anthropic's deployment from 1H 2027 and new Zen 6 EPYC chips are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: The growth story is strong, but the volatility (beta 2.45) and valuation make a large concentrated position risky.

gm.evidence: GAAP gross margin was 50% in 2025, and trailing gross margin was about 55.7% by mid-2026, high for hardware though below NVIDIA's.

fcfyield.evidence: Free-cash-flow yield was about 0.85% (P/FCF about 118) in October 2026, low even for its growth rate.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value of about $980B is roughly 150 times operating profit, an EBIT yield below 1%.

pa2.evidence: AMD is not in a setback; its shares and earnings are near record highs, apart from a cyclical drop in gaming revenue.

pa4.evidence: The business is financially safe with $13.1B cash vs $3.2B debt, but at about 155 times earnings the shares could fall a long way if AI growth slows.

wo1.evidence: AMD is the second-largest supplier of AI data-center accelerators and powers AI PCs and edge AI devices.

wo2.evidence: Each chip generation lowers cost per unit of compute, opening new AI demand, but AMD's own selling prices are rising rather than falling.

wo3.evidence: AMD's products serve AI across cloud, PCs, cars and robotics, but it is mostly a single AI-compute platform rather than several.

wo4.evidence: AMD expects the data-center AI accelerator market to exceed $1 trillion by 2030, growing above 45% a year.

ac3.evidence: AMD is exposed to US export controls (about $440M of MI308 charges in 2025), PC and gaming cycles, TSMC wafer and HBM memory costs, and AI capital-spending swings.

ns1.evidence: AMD competes on performance per dollar, but it is not the scale leader sharing savings in a way that locks out rivals; NVIDIA has more scale in AI.

ns4.evidence: If AI GPU deployments succeed, AMD will be much stronger than today, but rivals' custom chips and CUDA make that uncertain.

va2.evidence: It addresses the shortage and high cost of AI and cloud computing power, a problem worth hundreds of billions of dollars a year to its customers.
